messages.subject: using procD.lm and procD.pgls for non-coordinate data?
messages.subject_clean: using procD.lm and procD.pgls for non-coordinate data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,
I is there a way to use the 'procD.lm' and 'procD.pgls' for multivariate regressions of non-shape data (e.g,. PCs, or combinations of other variables).

I used to be able to use these functions (see below) with no problem:

'OLS_PCscores.data_lnCS <- procD.lm(means.data.PCscores[,4:45] ~ means.data.PCscores[,3], iter=1000, verbose=T)'

However, recently they stopped working when attempting to use 'regular' data instead of a 'geomorph data frame' with coords. I am now using the newer version of geomorph (3.0.5). Below is the error message, any advice would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,
Sergio

'Warning: no geomorph data frame provided.
      If an error occurs, this might be the reason.
Error in `$<-.data.frame`(`*tmp*`, "Y", value = c(-0.013397161322031,  :
  replacement has 55 rows, data has 0'

messages.body_plain:
Sergio,

Yes, procD.lm and procD.pgls may be used on non-shape data; either univariate or multivariate.

The error you have with 3.0.5 is because you did not use a geomorph data frame. If you create one of these containing your data, you are free to use shape or non-shape data in these functions.

Please carefully read the help files in geomorph for instructions of proper use and set up of data.

Best,

Dean

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Professor

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Subject: [geomorph-r-package] using procD.lm and procD.pgls for non-coordinate data?

Hi there,

I is there a way to use the 'procD.lm' and 'procD.pgls' for multivariate regressions of non-shape data (e.g,. PCs, or combinations of other variables).

I used to be able to use these functions (see below) with no problem:

'OLS_PCscores.data_lnCS <- procD.lm(means.data.PCscores[,4:45] ~ means.data.PCscores[,3], iter=1000, verbose=T)'

However, recently they stopped working when attempting to use 'regular' data instead of a 'geomorph data frame' with coords. I am now using the newer version of geomorph (3.0.5). Below is the error message, any advice would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,

Sergio

'Warning: no geomorph data frame provided.

      If an error occurs, this might be the reason.

Error in `$<-.data.frame`(`*tmp*`, "Y", value = c(-0.013397161322031,  :

  replacement has 55 rows, data has 0'

messages.body_plain:
It might be that you need to define shape as a matrix in your data frame, e.g.,

gdf2 <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = as.matrix(means.data.PCscores[,4:45]), …)

It could be that your original PC scores were a data frame, so they get treated as separate variables rather than a matrix.

I’m not sure if that will work, but it is worth a try.

Mike

messages.subject: Plotting options with procD.allometry?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Geomorph community,

This might be a simple r question, or it might be specific to geomorph; in any case pardon my ignorance as I'm fairly new to both r and geomorph. I have a figure (see below) and I am having some difficulty with reformatting it.

The code that generates the plot
par(cex.lab=1.5)
plot(mydata, method = "PredLine")
title('The effect of size on shape by population')

Using par(), I am able to adjust the axis label size using cex.lab and I can even increase the line size of the series elements and the graph box with lwd; but I have not figured out how to alter the series shape or element size.

In the above par(cex.lab=1.5) command, if I rerun the code with the following adjustments: par(cex.lab=1.5, pch=19, cex=2) it will produce the exact same figure (below). and if I look at all of the par() settings using par(no.readonly = T) - both pch and cex are set to the values I set despite the plot printing out pch = 5 and cex = 1 (that's my guess as I can't see if these are actually set to those values)

It was also be helpful to either mute the group text, or also change its size - but again I can't figure out how to do that either.

Any help in customizing this figure would be extremely appreciated as I've wasted several hours on this problem.

Thanks,
Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Plotting options with procD.allometry?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jeremy,

being a quick, automatic tool for reviewing allometric data, plot.procD.allometry has predefined options for the plotting arguments pch and cex which cannot be overridden.

For producing more elaborate graphs with specific plotting options, I would recommend using the predicted values provided in the output of the procD.allometry function ($pred.val component of the object) to build the plot by hand, with the graphic options you prefer.

All the best,
Antigoni

messages.subject: Intensity of Fluctuating Asymmetry
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues

I was wondering if anyone knows if there is a quantitative way to calculate the intensity of fluctuating asymmetry.

I’m aware that computing individual x side interaction in a Procrustes ANOVA is the standard manner to estimate if there is FA.  Nevertheless, I cannot understand what I have to do to compare FA levels in a quantitative way between –for example- different groups or populations (and which one have higher FA than other).

Is there any way to this and if there is, is it implement in geomorph package or other piece of software?

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Intensity of Fluctuating Asymmetry
messages.body_plain:
Hugo,

I have two suggestions.  First, if one were to take the fluctuating shape component for each individual, as found in the output of bilat.symmetry, one could then perform an anova using procD.lm to compare this among groups. That asks whether one group displays a greater degree of FA than another group.

Second, one could also perform a disparity analysis on the fluctuating shape component to determine whether there is greater variation in FA in one group relative to another.

I suspect that the second of these may be more informative. The anova-type analysis is a test of mean location, which makes a bit less sense using FA data, because one may not expect that the fluctuating shape components are all distinct from the grand mean in a particular direction in shape space (they are fluctuating after all). But it still may occur.

The second approach makes considerably more sense and tests whether levels of variation in FA differ among groups. This is far more intuitive, say if one is comparing FA variation in pristine vs. contaminated sites.

Hope this helps.

Dean

  emission

Emma

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Plotting ProcD.lm results
messages.body_plain:
The plot.procD.lm function has both PC and regression plotting options.  There are some examples in the procD.lm help file.  As every model is unique, so are the plotting options.  The PC plot will rotate your data space to align with the major axes of shape variation, as estimated by your model; i.e., a PCA of predicted values with projection of the observed values onto the PC axes.  The regression plot is much like the allometry plots in procD.allometry, except one can use a predictor other than shape.

All par options available to the plot function can be used with the plots to tailor the plots any way you like.

Hope that helps!

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Normalizing PCA from plotTangentSpace
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nils,

Because you volunteered being “not the best at R”, I’ll try to provide some help for not just this function but any R function that does the same thing.  plotTangentSpace is a function that has “ellipsis” programming.  What this means in R is that arguments in one function can be passed onto another function the first function uses.  For plotTangentSpace, we use prcomp, so the ellipsis programming (denoted as “…" in the arguments) allows any argument one might use in prcomp to also be used in plotTangentSpace.  Whenever you see “…” in an argument for an R function, it means there are other functions that can be manipulated by the main function.

For plotTangentSpace, you mentioned “normalizing” the PCA results and used a size = T argument to indicate your intention.  I think you meant standardizing the variables (to make a correlation matrix instead of a covariance matrix), which is scale. = T in prcomp.  Thus, you can do

myPCA <- plotTangentSpace(myCoords, .scale = T)

to accomplish this.  Realize that the warpgrids will not make much sense, as we do not have a step for un-standardizing the data, but the PC scores that result should be what you seek.  If this is not what you intended, then whichever prcomp argument you would like to change can be changed also in plotTangentSpace.

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Normalizing PCA from plotTangentSpace
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nils,

not sure what you mean by "normalizing" PCA results, do you want to center and scale the data? prcomp does not have, as far as I recall a "size" argument as your code suggests...

Anyway, if what you want to do is center and scale, yes, you can pass these prcomp arguments directly to plotTangentSpace, as the function uses prcomp under the hood. Caution is needed if you want to visualize the results in terms of shape variation, though, as centering shape data substracts the mean shape configuration from your coordinates. This means that after applying such a centering, your data will "loose" their geometric properties, and deformation grids will look weird. For visualization, you would need to add back the consensus to your pca data.

Not sure this is what you meant, though.
All the best,
Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Nils,

If you are using Procrustes methods, I do not think standardizing the Procrustes residuals is a smart thing to do.  If visualizing the shapes of specimens is important, do not standardize the variables and for the vegan Procrustes rotation you wish to do, just realize that you can standardize the variables to get the PC scores, if you want, but the warpgrids will not make sense.  They might make more sense if you multiplied the coordinates by their standard deviations and added the mean shape, as Antigoni mentioned before.  But this does not seem necessary for the analysis you wish to do.

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Normalizing PCA from plotTangentSpace
messages.body_plain:
Nils,

To respond to your question and follow up on Mike’s comment:  the discussion of to standardize or not standardize variables for PCA typically comes up with ecological data or other datasets where individual variables are being treated multivariately. Sometimes, such data contain variables that may be in different units and/or scale. This matters because some variables may have larger variation than others due simply to the fact that they were measured in those different units or scale. In such cases, those variables with excessively large variation due to scaling would then have ‘undue’ influence on the directions of the eigenvectors. This may not be desirable, and so standardization is used. A rather silly example is if one trait is measured in millimeters and the rest in meters.  The trait in mm will be expected to have variation 1000 times greater than the other traits simply due to the scale of the values, and would thus ‘pull’ the dominant eigenvector in its direction. This may not be desirable (and in this case also avoidable).

That being said however, standardization should not be thought of as an automatic operation. For instance, some data may be in similar units and scale and still display large variance disparities between traits. In these cases, standardization is actually bad as it obliterates the very variance-covariance patterns one wishes to summarize in the data!  As always, thinking is encouraged before applying some operation (standardization in this case).

Now for the case of Procrustes residuals, these are in the same units, and are in appropriate relative scale to one another. So there is no need to standardize these for PCA at all.

Hope this helps,

Dean

The warpgrids are based on mapping the reference configuration onto specimen configurations and correspond to a shape space that is not standardized.  I do not know of a theoretical treatment that standardizes shape spaces and do not wish to advocate this, for the purpose of visualizing shape variation.

Cheers!

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Normalizing PCA from plotTangentSpace
messages.body_plain:
One thing for our users to be careful of in this thread is the discussion of “Procrustes” methods.  In geomorph, gpagen does Procrustes superimposition of landmark configurations.  In vegan, the procrustes function performs a Procrustes rotation of one set of data to another.  This is typically done with ordination scores to see if two ordinations - e.g., PC projections - are similar.  A test is performed to ascertain whether the alignment is significant based on random alignments.  It is possible to perform a Procrustes rotation of e.g., shape data and behavior data.  Since these variables are measured with different units and different scales, scaling variables first might be wise.

I believe Nils is attempting something along these lines.

I recommend, however, using a two-block partial least squares analysis for this purpose.  It accomplishes the same goal without having to contrive reduced axes (Procrustes rotation is based on the smallest number of matching dimensions) or standardize variables.  Furthermore, the statistic is a correlation coefficient and the goal is to determine if data sets are correlated.  With the function in geomorph, the warp grids are also appropriate if some of the data are shape data.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Pst calculations
messages.body_plain:
Any thought on my last post, whether I am on the right track with the Pst calculations. I am especially interested if I am truly finding the Procrustes variance

Bjarni

On Sunday, July 9, 2017 at 4:15:09 PM UTC, bj...@mail.holar.is wrote:
> Hi all again
>
> I have again been visiting this, for the Pst calculations, and I am wondering if I am on the right track in finding the within and among population morphological variation to then further calculate Pst. I did not use residuals, but rather had size as a co-variant.
>
> This is what I have so far:
>
> morph.data<-readland.tps("jminjaw.tps")
> #read the landmarks back in (not a neccessary step, but I did it here because I had ran into trouble)
> define.sliders(morph.data,nsliders=6)
> #Defines the slider file - those files can be used multiple times, if the dataset is the same
> sliders<-read.csv("curveslide.csv")
> #Reads the slider file
> cave.gpa<-gpagen(morph.data,curves=sliders)
> #Runs a procrustes analysis
> groups <- read.csv("ID-June.csv", header=TRUE, sep=";")
> caves <- as.factor(groups$Cave)
> #Reading in a crouping variable and getting the grouping into the right format
> Datafr.gdf<-geomorph.data.frame(cave.gpa, caves=caves)
> #Here the co-ordinates are made into a dataframe
> procD.lm(coords~Csize,iter=999, data=Datafr.gdf)
> # Here the relationship between morphology and size are compared
> procD.lm(coords~Csize+caves,iter=999, data=Datafr.gdf)
> #here I test the differences among the caves with size as a covariant
> Morph.dis<-morphol.disparity(coords~Csize, groups=NULL, data=Datafr.gdf, iter=999)
> #Here I find the procrustes variance for the whole dataset, taking size into account
> Morph.disgroups<-morphol.disparity(coords~Csize*caves, groups=~caves, data=Datafr.gdf, iter=999)
> #Here I find the Procrustes variance for each cave and the distances among caves, taking size into account as co-variant
>
>
> Regarding the heritability, then I have been reading up on that.
>
> Here is a section from Mariani et al. 2012, which I have been looking at (Marine Ecology Progress Serise, 446:173-187),
>
> "A commonly applied alternative is the phenotypic ‘analogue’ PST, which is simply estimated from the between population (VB) and within population (VW) phenotypic components of variation (Merilä 1997). PST has often been used interchangeably with QST (Merilä & Crnokrak 2001, Leinonen et al. 2008), typically assuming c = 1 and h2 = 0.5 (Saether et al. 2007), where c is the between-population additive genetic component and h2 is the within-population additive genetic component (‘narrow-sense herit - ability’). However, recently, Brommer (2011) argued that, especially in cases of diversifying selection, environmental and non-additive genetic components of phenotypic variation among populations are likely to be substantial and, probably, much greater than h2 (rather than much less as assumed when equating PST directly with QST). Therefore, Brommer (2011) suggested the alternative formulation: PST = cVB / (cVB + 2h2 VW) (1) Rather than specific values of c and h2 (which are generally unknown) it is their ratio which determines whether conclusions that QST (estimated as PST) de viates from the null hypothesis provided by FST may be appropriately conservative; low values (e.g. c/h2 < 0.2) suggest more robust conclusions (Brommer 2011). Therefore, we first generated overall and pairwise PST estimates, and secondly determined the minimum value of c/h2 required for each phenotypic trait to produce non-overlapping confidence limits between PST and FST."
>
> I hope I am on the right track.
>
> Bjarni
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
> On Friday, March 24, 2017 at 8:59:51 AM UTC, bj...@mail.holar.is wrote:
> > Thank you for this Ian!!!
> >
> > Will look these up and see where they take me.
> >
> > Bjarni
> >
> > On Thursday, March 23, 2017 at 4:29:20 PM UTC, Ian Dworkin wrote:
> > > Bjarni
> > >
> > >  More generally I would suggest digging into the fairly deep literature on Fst VS. Qst (even while using the approach for Pst mentioned by Mike and Dean).  There is a lot there but a few citations like
> > >
> > >  S. Hoban, J. L. Kelley, K. E. Lotterhos, M. F. Antolin, G. Bradburd, D. B. Lowry, M. L. Poss, L. K. Reed, A. Storfer, and M. C. Whitlock, “Finding the Genomic Basis of Local Adaptation: Pitfalls, Practical Solutions, and Future Directions.,” Am Nat, vol. 188, no. 4, pp. 379–397, Oct. 2016.
> > >
> > >  T. Leinonen, R. J. S. McCairns, R. B. O'Hara, and J. Merilä, “QST–FST comparisons: evolutionary and ecological insights from genomic heterogeneity,” Nature Reviews Genetics, vol. 14, no. 3, pp. 179–190, Feb. 2013.
> > >
> > > M. C. Whitlock, “Evolutionary inference from QST,” Mol Ecol, vol. 17, no. 8, pp. 1885–1896, 2008.
> > >
> > >
> > > might be good places to start.
> > >
> > > On 23 March 2017 at 10:13, Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Bjarni,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I’ll add a few thoughts to what Mike suggested. First I will note though that the conundrum you are facing is directly analogous to the multivariate heritability issue faced some years ago in morphometrics, as I’ll explain below.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > For univariate data Pst is found as:  s^2_b / ( s^2_b + 2h^2 s^2_w)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > where the s^2_b is the between population variance, s^2_w is the within population variance, and h^2 is the heritability.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > For the multivariate case, as Mike mentioned the variance components are now covariance matrices, and there are two obvious ways to obtain a scalar estimate of Pst. One way is to use take the trace of each of these first.  Here, one has the total SS between and the total SS within.  One can obtain these easily from a Procrustes anova.  Note then that one still requires an estimate of heritability, or without these one at least can use a range of possible values.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > The alternative is to retain these as covariance matrices, perform the matrix computations, and then obtain the trace of the outcome. Like Mike I do not know if this will arrive at the same numerical value, but based on the multivariate heritability discussion some years ago, my suspicion is that they will not.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Now, the description of methods above is precisely that used in multivariate heritability back in the early 2000s. Monteiro and colleagues proposed using summed Procrustes distances to obtain SS, analogous to the Procrustes anova description above. Alternatively, Klingenberg proposed a full matrix approach, much like Mike and I mentioned (note: their joint paper in 2005 in Syst. Biol. describes the different perspectives and interpretations).  Some colleagues and I used both of these approaches in a 2006 empirical paper to compare them, and while estimates gave similar biological conclusions, there was more to be gained from the full multivariate approach in terms of understanding patterns of shape variation.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > So given that discussion on multivariate heritability, I agree with Mike and am inclined to suggest you retain things using full multivariate covariance matrices until the end of the procedure. That requires obtaining the between- and within-group covariance matrices from the manova SSCP, and using these for Pst estimates. The one complication that remains then is the heritability estimate. To generalize the Pst equation above, it seems that this would be represented as a p x p diagonal matrix, with the h^2 found on the diagonal.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > One final comment, I know of a paper that compared Fst and Pst where the latter were obtained from GM shape data (Leinonen et al 2006). However, they found Pst for the first PC and second PC of shape univariately, so I would not recommend their approach.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Leinonen, et. al. 2006. Contrasting patterns of body shape and neutral genetic divergence in marine and lake populations of threespine sticklebacks. J. Evol. Biol. 19: 1803–1812.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Good luck,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Dean
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Dr. Dean C. Adams
> > > >
> > > > Professor
> > > >
> > > > Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology
> > > >
> > > >        Department of Statistics
> > > >
> > > > Iowa State University
> > > >
> > > > www.public.iastate.edu/~dcadams/ <http://www.public.iastate.edu/~dcadams/>
> > > >
> > > > phone: 515-294-3834
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com [mailto:geomorph-...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Mike Collyer
> > > > Sent: Thursday, March 23, 2017 8:04 AM
> > > > To: bj...@mail.holar.is
> > > > Cc: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
> > > > Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Pst calculations
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Bjarni,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > This is a question I am less likely to give a good answer, as I do not fundamentally work in quantitative genetics or population genetics, but I’ll offer two routes to consider and let somebody else chime in if there is an ardent preference.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Procrustes variance is the sum of squared distances of observations from the mean, divided by degrees of freedom, irrespective of the number of dimensions of the tangent space.It can also be described as the trace of either a p x p covariance matrix or an n x n covariance matrix, where the former is found from the cross-products of variables and the latter from crossproducts of observations.  Either way, the trace is the same.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > The reason these alternative explanations is important is because how does one generalize the concept of Fst, Qst, or Pst for multivariate data?  Let’s use Qst for simplicity.  Qst = varB/(varB + 2*varW), where B and W represent between- and within-population additive genetic notation of variances.  If we use the trace of matrices B and W for covariance matrices to get Procrustes variances and there is only one variable, then the trace of the 1 x 1 covariance matrices is the variance for the single variable.  Thus, we arrive at the same answer.  Alternatively, if we calculate the matrix product (B + 2*W)^1 x B and take the trace of this covariance matrix product, which is a generalization of the formula, and if we have only one variable, then again, we get the same answer.  These are two generalizations that work for a single variable.  They also produce the same answer for multivariate data, as long as n degrees of freedom are used (where n is the number of observations).  I believe in Qst measurements, n is used for degrees of freedom in all cases.  If this is not the case, then the two generalizations might produce different answers.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I’m not sure if the two generalizations produce the same answer for Pst.  You might have to verify that, but if they don’t, I’m more inclined to favor the latter generalization (matrix product before trace), just because it is consistent with other statistical approaches.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Again, this is not in my wheelhouse, so somebody can probably shed better light on this than me.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > In geomorph, you can use residuals and fitted values from procD.lm or advanced.procD.lm to construct matrix products or feed them into morphol.disparity with the equation, e.g.,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > residuals ~ 1
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > which returns the Procrustes variance across all n values.  This should allow you to make these estimates.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Cheers!
> > > >
> > > > Mike
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Mar 23, 2017, at 8:06 AM,  bj...@mail.holar.is wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Hi Mike
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Thank you for this. I believe you answered my question. But I of-course have a follow up question. I am interested in the Fst values for the shape - Pst. The question is thus, how would I get those, using the Procrustes residuals in R?
> > > > >
> > > > > Bjarni
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thursday, March 23, 2017 at 10:40:13 AM UTC, Michael Collyer wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Bjarni,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Whether you calculate variance on Procrustes residuals projected into tangent space or all PC scores calculated from the same residuals makes no difference.  The variances are exactly the same.  If you are asking if you should use only one or a subset of available PCs, my response is don't do that.  There is no reason to do that.  The first PC, as a surrogate for shape, can miss important components of inter-specimen variation.  More importantly, if the first PC axis does not align well with population structure, you run the risk of making improper inferences.  For example, let’s say that the first PC just happens to be most associated with allometric variation in shape and the second PC with subpopulation variation.  If you use use first PC scores only, you miss the appropriate characterization of the population structure in your estimates.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thus, use the Procrustes residuals or all PC scores from them, unless you are not interested in Fst values for shape but are interested in some other trait that you have arbitrarily assigned as the first PC of shape variation.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Cheers!
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Mike
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Mar 23, 2017, at 3:33 AM, bj...@mail.holar.is <http://mail.holar.is/> wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Hi all
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I am studying morphological diversity among a number of small benthic populations found in Iceland.  One of the things we are interested in is comparisons of Fst and Pst values. For that I need to be able to calculate phenotypic variance within and among populations. Here I am stuck. Is there a way to calculate variance from the procrustes landmarks, or is it necessary for me to find first PCA axis and calculate variances of axis scores?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > All ideas appreciated.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Bjarni

Hi Mike,

I've looked at the two.b.pls <https://rdrr.io/cran/geomorph/man/two.b.pls.html> command from geomorph. It seems that it requires two 3D arrays for comparison. One of my data sets (the non-geomorph one) was based on euclidean measurements, not landmarks. So I was unable to make it into a 3D array. Would you know anyway to work around this?

Cheers,
Nils

On Thursday, 7 September 2017 17:47:17 UTC+1, Michael Collyer wrote:

> One thing for our users to be careful of in this thread is the discussion of “Procrustes” methods.  In geomorph, gpagen does Procrustes superimposition of landmark configurations.  In vegan, the procrustes function performs a Procrustes rotation of one set of data to another.  This is typically done with ordination scores to see if two ordinations - e.g., PC projections - are similar.  A test is performed to ascertain whether the alignment is significant based on random alignments.  It is possible to perform a Procrustes rotation of e.g., shape data and behavior data.  Since these variables are measured with different units and different scales, scaling variables first might be wise.
>
> I believe Nils is attempting something along these lines.
>
> I recommend, however, using a two-block partial least squares analysis for this purpose.  It accomplishes the same goal without having to contrive reduced axes (Procrustes rotation is based on the smallest number of matching dimensions) or standardize variables.  Furthermore, the statistic is a correlation coefficient and the goal is to determine if data sets are correlated.  With the function in geomorph, the warp grids are also appropriate if some of the data are shape data.
>
> Cheers!
> Mike

This matters because some variables may have larger variation than others due simply to the fact that they were measured in those different units or scale. In such cases, those variables with excessively large variation due to scaling would then have ‘undue’ influence on the directions of the eigenvectors. This may not be desirable, and so standardization is used. A rather silly example is if one trait is measured in millimeters and the rest in meters. messages.body_plain:
Hi Nils,

The function does not require 3D arrays.  It works with matrices.  Note the description from the function:

A1

A 3D array (p x k x n) containing GPA-aligned coordinates for the first block, or a matrix (n x variables)
A2

A 3D array (p x k x n) containing GPA-aligned coordinates for the second block, or a matrix (n x variables)
The function requires 3D arrays only if warpgrids are to be generated.

Mike

messages.subject: Interpreting slope vectors in advanced.procD.lm
messages.body_plain:
Hi Avi,

I cc’ed the google group on this reply so that others might benefit form the Q & A.

Please see responses below -Mike

>
> I'm having some difficulty with interpreting the slopes in the advanced.procD.lm. In the Value section it says that the first one is for magnitude differences, while the second is for differences in shape direction.
>
> What does the effect size and P of change in shape direction really tells me?
Slope vectors are vectors, and as vectors, they have a length (magnitude) and direction.  Two vectors can differ in one or both of these properties.  For shape allometry (slope) vectors, the length is the amount of shape change per unit of size change.  This has absolute meaning, as a length of 0 means no change.  Only in the case that the length is 0 would the direction also have absolute meaning (no direction).  Otherwise, it only has relative meaning.  The direction is relative contribution of changes in Cartesian coordinates for Procrustes residuals.  Think about this in terms of traveling on foot.  You can walk a km in any direction.  But walking a km due W is different than walking a km in a NNE direction.  In this case, while the length is the same, the directions describe quite different journeys.  Luckily, we have the poles and rotation of the earth to give us Cardinal directions.  Although the concept is the same in (tangent spaces of) shape spaces, we do not have a standard.  The allometry vectors describe covariances of shape change for groups, associated with one unit of size change, but the coordinates are arbitrarily chosen (e.g., by using the first specimen or PCs of the tangent space).  Nevertheless, regardless of the arbitrary definition of the coordinates, two vectors have the same spatial relationship to each other, even if one rotates the space.  Therefore, regardless of coordinate system, the correlation between vectors is a measure of their similarity to go off into similar directions in the tangent space from the starting point of the mean shape, as size increases.  The arccosine of the correlation is the angle between vectors, so this is more of a measure of difference in directions, as larger angles mean great difference.  Either way, as statistics, these values can be used to contrast the way shape changes (direction) rather than how much shape changes (magnitude), as the same amount of shape change can occur in much different ways.

> Should I report both effect sizes and P?
Yes.

> Is it possible to find significant differences only in one of them (magnitude or direction; regarding a specific couple), or if one of them is significant the other also has to be significant?
Yes, you can find changes in just one of the two attributes, which is why we provide results for both.

> > > One thing for our users to be careful of in this thread is the discussion of “Procrustes” methods.  In geomorph, gpagen does Procrustes superimposition of landmark configurations.  In vegan, the procrustes function performs a Procrustes rotation of one set of data to another.  This is typically done with ordination scores to see if two ordinations - e.g., PC projections - are similar.  A test is performed to ascertain whether the alignment is significant based on random alignments.  It is possible to perform a Procrustes rotation of e.g., shape data and behavior data.  Since these variables are measured with different units and different scales, scaling variables first might be wise.
> > >
> > > I believe Nils is attempting something along these lines.
> > >
> > > I recommend, however, using a two-block partial least squares analysis for this purpose.  It accomplishes the same goal without having to contrive reduced axes (Procrustes rotation is based on the smallest number of matching dimensions) or standardize variables.  Furthermore, the statistic is a correlation coefficient and the goal is to determine if data sets are correlated.  With the function in geomorph, the warp grids are also appropriate if some of the data are shape data.
> > >

> > > > Nils,
> > > >
> > > > To respond to your question and follow up on Mike’s comment:  the discussion of to standardize or not standardize variables for PCA typically comes up with ecological data or other datasets where individual variables are being treated multivariately. Sometimes, such data contain variables that may be in different units and/or scale. This matters because some variables may have larger variation than others due simply to the fact that they were measured in those different units or scale. In such cases, those variables with excessively large variation due to scaling would then have ‘undue’ influence on the directions of the eigenvectors. This may not be desirable, and so standardization is used. A rather silly example is if one trait is measured in millimeters and the rest in meters.  The trait in mm will be expected to have variation 1000 times greater than the other traits simply due to the scale of the values, and would thus ‘pull’ the dominant eigenvector in its direction. This may not be desirable (and in this case also avoidable).
> > > >
> > > > That being said however, standardization should not be thought of as an automatic operation. For instance, some data may be in similar units and scale and still display large variance disparities between traits. In these cases, standardization is actually bad as it obliterates the very variance-covariance patterns one wishes to summarize in the data!  As always, thinking is encouraged before applying some operation (standardization in this case).
> > > >
> > > > Now for the case of Procrustes residuals, these are in the same units, and are in appropriate relative scale to one another. So there is no need to standardize these for PCA at all.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mike,

Regarding the magnitude of shape changes (slope vectors), you said that: "The allometry vectors describe covariances of shape change for groups, associated with one unit of size change, but the coordinates are arbitrarily chosen (e.g., by using the first specimen or PCs of the tangent space)."

Is there any way to choose the coordinates by which individuals are being compared?
For instance, I want to compare the shape of a given trait among species but I know that one of the species is ancestral to all others. Can I use the ancestral species as the pivot around which all other species would be compared to? If yes, is there any way to implement that on geomorph?

Thank you in advance!
Cheers,
Alexandre

On Mon, Sep 11, 2017 7:34 AM, Mike Collyer  mlco...@gmail.com wrote:

> Hi Avi,
>
> I cc’ed the google group on this reply so that others might benefit form the Q & A.
>
> Please see responses below -Mike
>
> >
> > I'm having some difficulty with interpreting the slopes in the advanced.procD.lm. In the Value section it says that the first one is for magnitude differences, while the second is for differences in shape direction.
> >
> > What does the effect size and P of change in shape direction really tells me?
> Slope vectors are vectors, and as vectors, they have a length (magnitude) and direction.  Two vectors can differ in one or both of these properties.  For shape allometry (slope) vectors, the length is the amount of shape change per unit of size change.  This has absolute meaning, as a length of 0 means no change.  Only in the case that the length is 0 would the direction also have absolute meaning (no direction).  Otherwise, it only has relative meaning.  The direction is relative contribution of changes in Cartesian coordinates for Procrustes residuals.  Think about this in terms of traveling on foot.  You can walk a km in any direction.  But walking a km due W is different than walking a km in a NNE direction.  In this case, while the length is the same, the directions describe quite different journeys.  Luckily, we have the poles and rotation of the earth to give us Cardinal directions.  Although the concept is the same in (tangent spaces of) shape spaces, we do not have a standard.  The allometry vectors describe covariances of shape change for groups, associated with one unit of size change, but the coordinates are arbitrarily chosen (e.g., by using the first specimen or PCs of the tangent space).  Nevertheless, regardless of the arbitrary definition of the coordinates, two vectors have the same spatial relationship to each other, even if one rotates the space.  Therefore, regardless of coordinate system, the correlation between vectors is a measure of their similarity to go off into similar directions in the tangent space from the starting point of the mean shape, as size increases.  The arccosine of the correlation is the angle between vectors, so this is more of a measure of difference in directions, as larger angles mean great difference.  Either way, as statistics, these values can be used to contrast the way shape changes (direction) rather than how much shape changes (magnitude), as the same amount of shape change can occur in much different ways.
>
> > Should I report both effect sizes and P?
> Yes.
>
> > Is it possible to find significant differences only in one of them (magnitude or direction; regarding a specific couple), or if one of them is significant the other also has to be significant?
> Yes, you can find changes in just one of the two attributes, which is why we provide results for both.
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alexandre,

This is challenging but somewhat possible.  The default in gpagen is to align specimens to their first PCs.  Therefore, the resulting Procrustes coordinates are aligned to the principal axis of variation, and any coefficients in subsequent analyses represent departures - coordinate by coordinate - in the x, y, and possibly, z directions - from the starting position, which is the mean configuration aligned to its PCs.  You can align the mean to some other configuration, as long as it is the first specimen, by choosing PrinAxes = FALSE as one argument.

So, how to force alignment to an ancestral species or mean of a group or some other summary of more than one configuration?

Here is my recipe.

1. Perform GPA with PrinAxes = TRUE (or false, really does not matter).
2. Get the summary configuration (group mean: good example of that for coords.subset; ancestral state, maybe using ace from ape or designating one species; etc.)
3. Append this configuration to a new set of coordinates, which are the $coords from the gpagen object in step 1.  E.g.,

n <- dim(Y.gpa$coords)[[3]]
p <- dim(Y.gpa$coords)[[1]]
k <- dim(Y.gpa$coords)[[2]]
new.coords <- array(NA, c(p,k, (n+1) )
new.coords[,,1] <- summary.config # summary.config is from step 2
new.coords[,, (2:(n+1))] <- Y.gpa$coords

4. Perform gpagen on new.coords with PrinAxes = FALSE (aligns to first specimen).
5. Remove the first specimen from the $coords of the new gpagen object in 4
6. Perform gpagen again with PrinAxes = FALSE on the $coords from 5.

The alignment after 6 should have all of the specimens the same in a PC plot as after step 1, meaning nothing has changed.  However, when you use plotAllSpecimens, the rotation should be influenced by the first (summary) specimen in step 4.

An alternative way to do this if you are not averse to rotation calculations in R is to design a script to use a for loop or apply function and rotate all of the coords in a gpagen object to summary configuration.  This is easier, but assumes you know what you are doing with calculating cross-products and performing singular value decompositions to obtain rotation matrices.

Now that I have pointed out how to do this, conceptually, I am willing to predict that it is a rather useless exercise.  I’m not sure that it accomplishes much.  All analytical results would be exactly the same as if only step 1 is done, except that the coefficients of slope vectors look different.  The tables of pairwise statistics should be the same.  If one group in the table is the ancestral species, all pairwise stats that include that group are divergences from that ancestral species and will be the same whether the coordinate system is defined differently.

I hope that makes sense.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Alexandre,

Mike’s procedure, and subsequent comments are correct. But I wish to expound a bit on the latter.

Using a different reference for an aligned set of coordinates is akin to simply rotating the shape space to a new set of basis vectors (see Rohlf 1999). Thus, there is little to be gained here in terms of re-orienting the aligned shapes for this purpose as Mike stated. And because the amount of shape difference is defined by Procrustes = Euclidean distance, the distance between an ancestor vs. descendant is the same regardless of how one spins shape space (unlike using Manhattan distance; as is used in parsimony-based approaches).

So I agree 100% with Mike’s last comment that while it is possible to do such post-GPA rotations, there is little statistically to be gained here. And I would add that there is potentially something to be lost: additional calculations means more places where user errors can crop up; unnecessarily in this case.

Dean

> new.coords <- array(NA, c(p,k, (n+1) )
>

>

>

>
>
>

>

>
>

All analytical results would be exactly the same as if only step 1 is done, except that the coefficients of slope vectors look different.  The tables of pairwise statistics should be the same.  If one group in the table is the ancestral species, all pairwise stats that include that group are divergences from that ancestral species and will be the same whether the coordinate system is defined differently.

messages.subject: How is the variance in "points.var" of gpagen calculated?
messages.subject_clean: How is the variance in "points.var" of gpagen calculated?
messages.body_plain:
How is the variance among landmark points calculated after Procrustes superposition using the function gpagen. In other words where do the values in the component “point.var” in the gpagen object come from.

I conducted a Procrustes superposition (gpagen) on the example plethodon landmark data of the package (looking only at the landmarks of the Jord species).

I then compared the output of the “points.var” with a calculation of the standard deviation for all 12 landmarks in the x direction among all 20 species, and the same for the y direction. These numbers are not the same, hence the variance depicted in “points.var” is not the standard deviation or standard error. So, my question is, what is it.

Big thanks for any insights. Below is my code:

# the data

data(plethodon)

Res <- plethodon$land

index <- which(dimnames(Res)[[3]] =="Jord")

Res.jord <- Res[,,index]

# Procrustes analysis

PA <- gpagen(Res.jord)

PA$points.var       # variance coming from the GPA

# my own calculation of variation

Sd.x <- NULL

Sd.y <- NULL

for (l in 1:dim(Res)[1]){

Sd.x    <- c(Sd.x, sd(PA$coords [l, 1,]))

 Sd.y    <- c(Sd.y, sd(PA$coords [l, 2,]))

}

cbind(Sd.x, Sd.y)  # the variance I calculated, not the same.

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] How is the variance in "points.var" of gpagen calculated?
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] How is the variance in "points.var" of gpagen calculated?
messages.body_plain:
Standard deviation is the square root of variance.

The $pt.var calculation uses population variance (divided by n), not sample variance (divided by n - 1), as it references the population of configurations in GPA and not a sample of them.  Your use of sd assumes they are a sample.  Finally, the calculation does not re-center the values, as they have already been centered by subtracting the consensus configuration.  The sd function will assume they have not been centered and will center them.  This should have no effect but could lead to rounding error differences.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am looking at allometry patterns in cranial shape and am playing around with proc.d.allometry but I am not entirely sure I am interpreting all the ANOVA results I am looking at correctly. I have a group factor ("species") and was wondering what the correct way to interpret the p-values for size and for species would be. How may I compare the respective influence on shape of species and size (if at all)?

Sorry if this seems a silly question, and thanks in advance!

messages.body_plain:
Avi,

Never when comparing slope vectors would I say shapes are different.  If vectors are significantly different in magnitude or direction, then one can say that the groups compared have different allometries, and then focus on whether they differ because of the amount of shape change or the way shape changes, respectively, with size change.  I recommend abandoning the urge to compare shapes when comparing allometric vectors.  Shapes are locations in the tangent space, vectors are vectors.  They describe shape change, not shape.

Cheers!
Mike

> > Just to be sure, regarding the magnitude and direction of the vectors: It's enough that one of them is significantly different to state that the shapes are different, right (but I have to report that only in that parameter)?
> > Avi

> > On Mon, Sep 11, 2017 at 1:34 PM, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > Hi Avi,
> > >
> > > I cc’ed the google group on this reply so that others might benefit form the Q & A.
> > >
> > > Please see responses below -Mike
> > >
> > > >
> > > > I'm having some difficulty with interpreting the slopes in the advanced.procD.lm. In the Value section it says that the first one is for magnitude differences, while the second is for differences in shape direction.
> > > >
> > > > What does the effect size and P of change in shape direction really tells me?
> > > Slope vectors are vectors, and as vectors, they have a length (magnitude) and direction.  Two vectors can differ in one or both of these properties.  For shape allometry (slope) vectors, the length is the amount of shape change per unit of size change.  This has absolute meaning, as a length of 0 means no change.  Only in the case that the length is 0 would the direction also have absolute meaning (no direction).  Otherwise, it only has relative meaning.  The direction is relative contribution of changes in Cartesian coordinates for Procrustes residuals.  Think about this in terms of traveling on foot.  You can walk a km in any direction.  But walking a km due W is different than walking a km in a NNE direction.  In this case, while the length is the same, the directions describe quite different journeys.  Luckily, we have the poles and rotation of the earth to give us Cardinal directions.  Although the concept is the same in (tangent spaces of) shape spaces, we do not have a standard.  The allometry vectors describe covariances of shape change for groups, associated with one unit of size change, but the coordinates are arbitrarily chosen (e.g., by using the first specimen or PCs of the tangent space).  Nevertheless, regardless of the arbitrary definition of the coordinates, two vectors have the same spatial relationship to each other, even if one rotates the space.  Therefore, regardless of coordinate system, the correlation between vectors is a measure of their similarity to go off into similar directions in the tangent space from the starting point of the mean shape, as size increases.  The arccosine of the correlation is the angle between vectors, so this is more of a measure of difference in directions, as larger angles mean great difference.  Either way, as statistics, these values can be used to contrast the way shape changes (direction) rather than how much shape changes (magnitude), as the same amount of shape change can occur in much different ways.
> > >
> > > > Should I report both effect sizes and P?
> > > Yes.
> > >
> > > > Is it possible to find significant differences only in one of them (magnitude or direction; regarding a specific couple), or if one of them is significant the other also has to be significant?
> > > Yes, you can find changes in just one of the two attributes, which is why we provide results for both.
> > >

I came back to this topic for 2 reasons. The first and most important is that there is a rather strange result when I perform a PCA on my procD.allometry residuals. Here is what I did:

messages.body_plain:
Sérgio,

You have removed a common allometric effect AND SPECIES effects from your shapes and then were surprised that the PC plot did not reveal species differences.  Your allometry analysis revealed that species have a common allometry but also impressively large species differences in shape, given this common allometry; i.e., the intercepts for the species are quite varied.  The differences between the PC plots and their explained variation along axes emphasizes that in one case you removed species effects and in the other you didn’t.  In the latter, the first PC accounts for more variation because there are inherently large differences in shape among species.  If your intent is to visualize species differences with a PC plot, you should not have ~gp in the formula to remove the common allometry, or you should perform a PCA on the fitted values rather than the residuals.

Regarding the bug you think you found, I admit that it is a misleading error message.  The error is because you have negative size values.  The error message assumes that this happened because of transformation rather than you actually using a size variable that has negative values.  We will have to update the error message, but the error is simply because we have a trap for any negative values for size.  This is not a bug.  Size cannot be negative.

Cheers,
Mike

Geometric Morphometrics Using R (GMMR01)

https://www.prstatistics.com/course/geometric-morphometrics-using-r-gmmr01/

This course is being delivered by Prof. Dean Adams, Prof. Michael Collyer and Dr. Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou

This course will run from 19th – 23rd February 2018 at Margam Discovery Centre, Wales, UK.

The field of geometric morphometrics (GM) is concerned with the quantification and analysis of patterns of shape variation, and its covariation with other variables. Over the past several decades these approaches have become a mainstay in the field of ecology, evolutionary biology, and anthropology, and a panoply of analytical tools for addressing specific biological hypotheses concerning shape have been developed. The goal of this is to provide participants with a working knowledge of the theory of geometric morphometrics, as well as practical training in the application of these methods.

The course is organized in both theoretical and practical sessions. The theoretical sessions will provide a comprehensive introduction to the methods of landmark-based geometric morphometrics, which aims at providing the participants with a solid theoretical background for understanding the procedures used in shape data analysis. Practical sessions will include worked examples, giving the participants the opportunity to gain hands-on experience in the treatment of shape data using the R package geomorph. These sessions focus on the generation of shape variables from primary landmark data, the statistical treatment of shape variation with respect to biological hypotheses, and the visualization of patterns of shape variation and of the shapes themselves for interpretation of statistical findings, using the R language for statistical programming. While practice datasets will be available, it is strongly recommended that participants come with their own datasets.

Note: Because this is a geometric morphometrics workshop in R, it is required that participants have some working knowledge in R. The practical sessions of the course will focus on GM-based analyses, and not basic R user-interfacing. It is therefore strongly recommended that participants refresh their R skills prior to attending the workshop.

Hello everyone,

I'm somewhat a (advanced) beginner to R and definitely new to geomorph, so sometimes small issues can be quite challenging and demanding.
The issue I'm currently stuck with is related to the definition of semilandmarks using define.sliders. I've attached a TPS file containing a subset of my dataset of coordinates, which I've managed to import to R and calculate GPA alignment considering all coordinates as landmarks:

# Read tps file
land <-  readland.tps("ShapeTPS.tps", specID = "ID")

# Generalized Procrustes analysis without sliders
gpa <- gpagen(land,PrinAxes=FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)

However, when I try to define the semilandmarks automatically, it doesn't work and R returns the error "Error in La.svd(MY, k, k) : infinite or missing values in 'x'".

# Define sliders
sliders = rbind(define.sliders(1:27), define.sliders(27:52))

# Generalized procrustes analysis considering semilandmarks
gpa <- gpagen(land,PrinAxes=FALSE, print.progress = FALSE, curves = sliders)

I believe there is an issue with my result of define.sliders, as my matrix looks odd compared to the examples available:
> head(sliders)
     before slide after
[1,]      1     2     3
[2,]      2     3     4
[3,]      3     4     5

[5,]      5     6     7
[6,]      6     7     8

Using the image attached as reference, I'd like points 1 and 27 to be fixed landmarks, whereas 2:26 and 28:52 are meant to slide.

Given that it is possible to define the semilandmarks automatically, I'd rather not have to do it manually.

I'll appreciate any help.

messages.body_plain:
Pedro,

The problem is definitely with your data and how it was acquired: it is not a problem with gpagen.

After much digging I found at least one problem: specimen 32 has several landmarks which have precisely the same x & y coordinates. Having two landmarks in the same configuration with identical coordinates will cause all sorts of issues computationally: for instance, the tangents for sliding will be undefined, which will cause the numerical analyses based on those tangents to not be completed.

Then one must ask what it means biologically (or in any quantitative context) to have the same coordinates for ‘different’ anatomical landmarks in the same shape configuration.  That doesn’t seem to make any conceptual sense either.

Note that there may be other specimens further in the dataset with similar issues; I stopped looking for you once I identified this one.

I suggest you refine your automated landmarking procedure, as it does not appear to be fool-proof.

Dean

I managed to define the semilandmarks using the random landmark data, so I agree that there is an issue with my data.

land<-matrix(rnorm(52*2*56),ncol=2)

land<-arrayspecs(land,p=52,k=2)

sliders = rbind(define.sliders(1:27), define.sliders(c(27:52,1)))

gpaSLM <- gpagen(land,PrinAxes=FALSE, print.progress = FALSE, curves = sliders)

Call:

gpagen(A = land, curves = sliders, PrinAxes = FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)

Generalized Procrustes Analysis

with Partial Procrustes Superimposition

2 fixed landmarks

50 semilandmarks (sliders)

2-dimensional landmarks

6 GPA iterations to converge

The shape I'm analyzing is a cross correlation with some energy graphs (it can be though as a level curve in a mountain peak). The y coordinates of landmarks are calculated using energy from south to north (minimum to maximum y values) of the "mountain". For each calculated y value, I have two correlated x values in the level curve, except for the minimum and maximum y values, which have one correlated x value each.

Therefore, all x and y values in my landmark data are automatically calculated and their acquisition order is always the same (Max y value, decreasing y with correlated x1, min y value, increasing y values with correlated x2). I checked all of my images and the landmarks are definitely in the same order. I've even tried to change the order, but it returned the same error (see new polygon attached).

I looked into the gpagen function but failed to understand what is causing the error, or how could I go around it. If the problem is truly with how I'm acquiring my data, then I would probably need to go back to square one...However, I do believe there is a way of adapting gpagen to my data, we just need to figure out how.

Any thoughts?

messages.subject: geomorph update
messages.body_plain:
Colleagues,

We have made two small updates to geomorph which we wish to bring to your attention. Both are rather specialized and may affect only a small subset of users, however we wanted to alert everyone just in case.

First, a recent change to the underlying code in procD.fit inadvertently precluded use of weights or offsets in model fitting. This programming bug has now fixed.

Second, we have corrected an issue identified when 3+ partitions were used in integration.test and when the first partition contained variables which were not contiguous in the data.frame. Thanks to Zac Selden for identifying the issue.

Both changes have been made on github, and the updated version of geomorph may be installed as:

devtools::install_github(“geomorphR/geomorph”,ref=”Stable”).

Dean and the geomorph team

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Professor

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike and Dean,

I have a follow-up question. If I want to know if there are significant differences between taxa after accounting for sex, am I supposed to obtain pairwise comparisons like this:

my.procD <- advanced.procD.lm(coords ~ sex, ~ sex + taxon,

                              groups = ~taxon,
                              iter=999, data = procD.df)

or like this

my.procD <- advanced.procD.lm(coords ~ 1, ~ sex + taxon,

                              groups = ~taxon,
                              iter=999, data = procD.df)

In one the simpler model is a dimorphism model. In the other, and intercept model. The pairwise differences between taxa are significant for one advanced function (intercept model) but not the other (dimorphism model). I'd also like to understand why this is the case. I suspect the first model above is the correct one.

Thanks, guys.

David

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] procD.lm and advanced.procD.lm
messages.body_plain:
David,

The former approach accounts for sex the latter approach does not (and only accounts for the overall mean).  Whenever a simpler null model (like the intercept model is used) the effects sizes for test statistics (pairwise difference in means, in this case) will likely be larger but misrepresentative.  The reason is, using this example, that differences between males could contribute to differences between taxa, especially if the design is not balanced (i.e., one taxon is more represented by females and one more by males) and if sexual dimorphism is a strong effect.  Also, sexual dimorphism might vary among taxa (a sex * taxa effect is significant), potentially influencing a spurious result, if not accounted for.

Your first approach is fine as long as you are not concerned about sexual dimorphism varying among taxa.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm getting a warning message with the comparative methods.

> procD.pgls(shape ~ log(cs), phy = phy, data = gdfPGLS, iter = 9999, RRPP = FALSE,print.progress = FALSE)

Call:
procD.pgls(f1 = shape ~ log(cs), phy = phy, iter = 9999, RRPP = FALSE,      data = gdfPGLS, print.progress = FALSE)

Type I (Sequential) Sums of Squares and Cross-products
Randomization of Raw Values used
10000 Permutations

           Df         SS         MS     Rsq      F         Z Pr(>F)
log(cs)     1 0.00037645 0.00037645 0.22198 46.791 -0.064039 0.5185
Residuals 164 0.00131941 0.00000805
Total     165 0.00169586
Warning message:
In procD.pgls(shape ~ log(cs), phy = phy, data = gdfPGLS, iter = 9999,  :
  Singular phylogenetic covariance matrix. Proceed with caution

Do you know what does this warning mean? Does it mean I have only 1 tree and that I should use a multiPhylo? I tried multiPhylo and it didn't work, as only phylo works.
I did this with a different tree before but I don't understand which could be the difference.

Thanks in advance.

Best regards,
Sérgio Cardoso.

messages.body_plain:
Sergio,

It is simply a warning message, not an error message.  It means that the phylogenetic covariance matrix is not full rank.  When calculating this matrix, some of the covariances that should be positive are near 0 (maybe because of tree polytomies).

The analysis worked but alerted you that you covariance matrix was singular, just in case that is a surprise.

Mike

messages.subject_clean: Balanced design and advanced.procD.lm with groups
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I was searching this forum and the quick guide, but couldn't find answers to these two questions:
Should I treat the ANOVA functions as parametirc or a-parametirc? And can they deal with balanced and non-balanced design? I found these <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/geomorph-r-package/O8r5c-e9xJM/kdkDM3e5AwAJ> three <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/geomorph-r-package/34d5YIEzaCY/5NJvcmPoAQAJ> messages <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/geomorph-r-package/QxvaUFKF9Dk/-_--zejPAQAJ> but couldn't deduce from them.
Whenever I use advanced.procD.lm with groups, the Z and sig. never change by much (if it's the same group) from one models comparison to another. So if the general test isn't significant, I should clearly abandon the groups pairwise (whether by LS means or vector slopes). But why do the groups pairwise Z and sig. never change as much as (or according to) the general test Z and sig.?

Can anyone help?
Thanks,
Avi

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] procD.pgls - Warning message: Singular phylogenetic covariance matrix. Proceed with caution
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] procD.pgls - Warning message: Singular phylogenetic covariance matrix. Proceed with caution
messages.body_plain:
Sérgio,

Just so you are aware, if you have a balanced design (same number of tips per species), using species means should give you about the same answer.  We are able to handle singular matrices by using a phylogenetic projection matrix, derived from eigen-analysis.  (The projection matrix has lower rank than the number of tips, and should have rank that is about or exactly the same as the number of species.)  If your design in imbalanced, the result might change.

Normally, PGLS is done with tips equal to the number of species, perhaps using species means.  You have stumbled into a reality that exists but has not been explored, theoretically (although we are in the process of doing that).  If you know what you are doing, you can use weighted species means rather than just means, if imbalance is a concern.  Again, the theoretical justification of this using the permutation procedures we use has not been explored.  But also the polytomy approach you are using has not been explored.  One might argue that using this approach is tantamount to pseudoreplication, as statistical power might increase simply by over-representing species (without really increasing the effect size).

In your case you have a large F but a small effect size (Z) and the effect is not significant.  This is a strange result and makes me wonder if RRPP is actually robust to attempted pseudoreplication.  Regardless, for your empirical results, I’m not sure adding polytomies helped much.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Avi,

Regarding the second question, the overall group effect size will generally be larger than the pairwise groups sizes because it is a composite of all the pairwise effects.  The only way the effect size would be the same is there are only two groups.  The overall effect size for groups could be large if all pairwise effect sizes are moderate or could be large if most pairwise effects are small but maybe a couple of them are large.

The overall group effect size is basically a measure associated with the spread of group means.  There are different ways to make that large.  Small dispersion between groups but lots of dispersion when considering all groups is one way for that to manifest.

Mike

As I'll compute a mean shape per each species, I don't think weighted means would help a lot (I guess it would be more useful to create a mean shape of the species of a group, given an unbalanced design). In fact I ran the analysis with a brlen=1 (and no politomies) and the result is completely different.
>

>

> Sérgio.

On Tuesday, 26 September 2017 14:33:19 UTC+2, Michael Collyer wrote:

> Sérgio,
>
> Just so you are aware, if you have a balanced design (same number of tips per species), using species means should give you about the same answer.  We are able to handle singular matrices by using a phylogenetic projection matrix, derived from eigen-analysis.  (The projection matrix has lower rank than the number of tips, and should have rank that is about or exactly the same as the number of species.)  If your design in imbalanced, the result might change.
>
> Normally, PGLS is done with tips equal to the number of species, perhaps using species means.  You have stumbled into a reality that exists but has not been explored, theoretically (although we are in the process of doing that).  If you know what you are doing, you can use weighted species means rather than just means, if imbalance is a concern.  Again, the theoretical justification of this using the permutation procedures we use has not been explored.  But also the polytomy approach you are using has not been explored.  One might argue that using this approach is tantamount to pseudoreplication, as statistical power might increase simply by over-representing species (without really increasing the effect size).
>
> In your case you have a large F but a small effect size (Z) and the effect is not significant.  This is a strange result and makes me wonder if RRPP is actually robust to attempted pseudoreplication.  Regardless, for your empirical results, I’m not sure adding polytomies helped much.
>
> Cheers!
> Mike

messages.body_plain:
Sarah,

An error like this happens because the number of observations in the morphdisp.pgls analysis and sizecat differ, at least at the point R is making this calculation; i.e., it could be an internal problem that causes the number of observations to differ.  This error occurs before weights are incorporated, so I think the weights fix is just a coincidence.  Why it worked before and does not now, I am not sure.  First question, how recently did you update geomorph from Github or did you download it from CRAN?  If the latter, updating it from Github might be the best first step.  We made some updates recently that might be related to this issue.  If you update from Github and the problem persists, then we will have to diagnose it with your data.

If you have not downloaded geomorph from Github for a while, please do that, try running the code again, and alert me if you still have the error, this time sending your script and data to me directly (not the google group).

Good luck!
Mike

I add part of my communication with Mike (with minor changes) to share the discussion and maybe get other perspectives that will help me to better understand.
I used slopes instead of LS means since I added log(cs) as covariate. I thought that's the way to do it with covariate.
I'm mostly still puzzled with the groups effect sizes. Shouldn't they change much more (among tests) if the general test effect size has greatly changed (although it's the exact same groups)?
I'll be happy to hear any idea. Meanwhile, as Mike suggested me, I'll continue to dig in this forum archive.
Thanks a lot,
Avi

Hi Mike,
Thank you so much for your quick and detailed answer.
My primer goal is to test whether phenotypic plasticity exists between different types of habitats (lotic/lentic) by crossing them with different kind of treatments (flow/nonflow). I tested this hypothesis by quantifying the amount of change in shape as a function of treatment, type (of habitat) and time (before/after treatment). Using log(cs) as covariate was meant to control for the initial differences in size among larvae from different females. Some of the tests I did meant to test one factor effect only, given the other factors effects. Others only the interaction effect.
If I understand correctly, then if genotype is what matters, the test (shape ~ log(cs)+treat+time, ~ log(cs)+type+treat+time) should be significant. If only environment affects shape, then (shape ~ log(cs)+type+time, ~ log(cs)+type+treat+time) should be significant. Interaction only: (shape ~ log(cs)+type+treat+time, ~ log(cs)+type*treat+time).
Am I getting this wrong? I'm mostly still puzzled with the groups effect sizes. Shouldn't they change much more (among tests) if the general test effect size has greatly changed (although it's the exact same groups)?
Many thanks,
Avi

Avi,

It seems to me that you are trying to compare group means but setting up the analysis to compare allometric slopes (but not setting it up correctly for that either).  I suspect that you are too deep into trying to figure out analyses and I question if you fully understand the concepts for your analyses. This creates a quagmire where every attempt to fix or change an analysis is not clear in concept or process.

We have discussed this a lot in the forum - you can check the archives.  We have articles about these topics - you can review those.

Yes, you are isolating the “type” factor in your analysis but if that is the case, I’m not sure why you are comparing slopes.  This is why I question if it is a procedural issue or a conceptual one.

Mike

> Regarding the second question, the overall group effect size will generally be larger than the pairwise groups sizes because it is a composite of all the pairwise effects.  The only way the effect size would be the same is there are only two groups.  The overall effect size for groups could be large if all pairwise effect sizes are moderate or could be large if most pairwise effects are small but maybe a couple of them are large.
>
> The overall group effect size is basically a measure associated with the spread of group means.  There are different ways to make that large.  Small dispersion between groups but lots of dispersion when considering all groups is one way for that to manifest.

messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I am attempting to perform a procD.pgls analysis, but I am getting this error message:

>pgls <- procD.pgls(shape ~ range), phy = tree, data = gdf, iter =999, RRPP = TRUE)
Error in x[phy$tip.label, ] : subscript out of bounds

I think this is saying that the phylo tips are not matching the geomorph data frame. I tried uploading a TPS file with just genus and species names (separated by "_"), and phylogenetic analyses work just fine (e.g., plotGMPhyloMorphoSpace), but if I add any other variables to the same TPS file (also separated by "_" between each variable; the genus & species names remain the same in both files) , then they no longer work. I am using the strsplit(dimnames(crania)[[3]], "_" function to separate the variables in a classifiers data frame (as suggested here: https://github.com/geomorphR/geomorph/wiki/How-to-extract-classifiers-from-names-of-specimens) in order to make a geomorph data frame.

Does anyone have any ideas on what I am doing wrong, or how to match the phylogeny to a TPS file with variables included?

Thanks in advance for your help.

-Evan

messages.body_plain:
Evan,

One possibility is that base-R does not like names of the latter format (though I cannot confirm this).  More likely is that the names in the phylogeny  (phy$tip.labels) do not match the rownames in the data matrix.

As Mike suggested this is likely a mismatch between taxa names on the phylogeny and those in the data frame.  Unfortunately, we are simply not clairvoyant enough to know how to write code to account for all possible permutations of how users input their data and their phylogeny relative, and using what names. To see if you have some sort of mismatch try a simple:

match(rownames(data),phy$tip.labels)

If this shows anything other than a perfect 1:1 correspondence, then it is an input error.  If there is a perfect 1:1 correspondence, then something else is amiss.

Dean

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Phylogenetic Analyses
messages.body_plain:
Evan,

Since this is an I/O error, the simplest solution is to change the names in the data matrix so that they match those in the phylogeny. This may be done either inside or outside of R.

This is often handled outside of R entirely, and in the environment where the datafiles were originally generated. In your case, changing the specimen names by hand in the NTS file to match how they are named in the phylogeny would be efficiently accomplished in a text editor (if I may guess the NTS has image names and these do not match the names in the phylogeny?).

In the future if one ensures a 1: correspondence of image/specimen names with the species names listed in the phylogeny, many downstream headaches can be avoided.

Best,

Dean

I really appreciate your responses. I've been attempting to reenter (and reenter again) the names, copying them directly from the nexus file phylogeny, and I'm still running into the same problem. I'm hoping that if I provide more complete code (on a reduced version of the dataset, for ease), someone will be able to see where I am going astray.

When using a file with just genus and species, the procD.pgls works great:

library(geomorph)

> crania <- readland.nts(file.choose())

> categories <- strsplit(dimnames(crania)[[3]], "_")

> classifiers <- matrix(unlist(categories), ncol=2, byrow=T)

> classifiers <- cbind(dimnames(crania)[[3]], classifiers)

> colnames(classifiers) <- c("fileID", "Genus", "Species")

> classifiers <- as.data.frame(classifiers)

> classifiers

                       fileID                                              Genus                                   Species

1 Allenopithecus_nigroviridis                      Allenopithecus                  nigroviridis

2 Cercocebus_galeritus                                 Cercocebus                        galeritus

3 Cercocebus_torquatus                              Cercocebus                        torquatus

4 Cercopithecus_ascanius                            Cercopithecus                   ascanius

> Y.gpa<-gpagen(crania)

> tree <- read.nexus(file.choose())

Phylogenetic tree with 4 tips and 3 internal nodes.

[1] "Allenopithecus_nigroviridis" "Cercopithecus_ascanius"

[3] "Cercocebus_galeritus"        "Cercocebus_torquatus"

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Phylogenetic Analyses
messages.body_plain:
Evan,

This is what I’ve been trying to explain.  The names in both the phylogeny and the data matrix must match exactly.  When you add ‘_3’ to the data matrix names, they are now not the same as in the phylogeny. It will never work because the 2 cannot be made to match.

It is also not obvious why one must add something to the names to begin with. If these are some sort of independent (X) variables, they may be used in the data matrix for quantitative analysis. Adding them to the names will not change the analysis at all; other than, in this case, causing it not to run.

Dean
